methodological_rigor.justification: Single-center retrospective cohort with 1:1 propensity score matching (caliper 0.20, AUC 0.787) is an appropriate design for the exploratory comparison but cannot support causal claims about RPD superiority. Important residual confounding is explicitly acknowledged by the authors: chronological bias (RPD introduced in 2020, enrollment 2017–2025), a markedly higher proportion of trainee-performed cases in the OPD group (noted as 'major cofounder'), and expanding RPD indications over time. No a priori sample size/power calculation is reported, no handling of missing data is described, and no sensitivity analyses (e.g., alternate matching ratios, E-value, time-stratified comparison) are offered to probe robustness. The multivariable logistic regression for TO reports OR/95% CI but includes no adjustment for multiplicity across the univariate screen and no checks for calibration, interaction, or overfitting given ~255 events.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The study is an individual retrospective cohort with propensity score matching from a single high-volume center, mapping to Oxford LoE 2b. The question (short-term outcomes of RPD vs OPD and TO as a composite quality metric) is clinically important to hepatobiliary surgery, and the magnitude of improvements (hospital stay 13 vs 22 days, major complications 17.1% vs 44.4%) is practice-relevant for centers already pursuing robotic programs. However, endpoints are short-term/composite surrogates (TO within 1 month, no OS/PFS/QoL) and generalizability is limited by the single-center, expert-proctor setting with explicit selection restrictions (no vascular resection in RPD per Japanese reimbursement). The findings support ongoing adoption and training initiatives rather than changing standards of care.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE applies as this is an observational single-center cohort. Most core STROBE items are addressed: setting, participants, variables, data sources, statistical methods, descriptive and outcome tables, and a candid limitations paragraph. Gaps include absence of a participant flow diagram, no explicit handling of missing data, no clear a priori outcome specification, no exact definitions for inclusion/exclusion beyond the time window, and no mention of protocol registration. Data availability is weak: no statement in the retained text about repository deposition, code sharing, or availability of individual-level data on request, and analyses are reported as performed in an outdated JMP v11 without reproducible scripts.

novelty_literature.justification: The study is an incremental empirical contribution. Multiple prior PSM comparisons and two meta-analyses of RPD vs OPD are cited [26,31,32], and TO after robotic PD has been examined in prior cohorts [22,33]. The main 'novel' claim—that robotic surgery is an independent predictor of TO—is a modest extension of these prior analyses in a Japanese high-volume center that followed the LAELAPS-3 training pathway. No new mechanism, assay, trial design, or underserved population is introduced; the positioning is honest but does not credibly fill a documented gap beyond regional/center-level confirmation.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is generally readable and conventionally organized (introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusions), and the abstract is quantitatively grounded and consistent with the results. Weaknesses include a typographical error ('cofounder' for 'confounder'), some repetition between abstract/discussion/conclusions, and a benchmark comparison (Table 4) that is descriptively narrated without clearly defined matching of case mix. The methods are concise but under-specified in places (e.g., how pancreatic texture was assessed intraoperatively, surgeon-level clustering), and figure/table captions are serviceable rather than fully self-contained.

key_strengths: Clinically meaningful short-term differences (operative time, blood loss, LOS, major complications, CR-POPF) favoring RPD both before and after 1:1 PSM with AUC 0.787
Explicit, standardized surgical and ERAS protocols with training grounded in LAELAPS-3
Benchmark comparison (Table 4) that situates center performance against published RPD cohorts
Candid limitations section that names chronological bias, trainee imbalance, and selection bias
key_concerns: Severe residual confounding—RPD performed almost exclusively by a proctor/board-certified experts while OPD disproportionately included surgical trainees; this alone could drive the observed advantage
Chronological bias (RPD 2020–2025 vs OPD 2017–2025) with evolving perioperative care, not adjusted for in the matching model
No power/sample-size justification, no handling of missing data, no sensitivity analyses, and no multiplicity correction across the predictor screen for TO
Novelty is incremental—prior PSM studies and meta-analyses already report similar RPD advantages; TO as endpoint has been examined before
Weak reporting of data/code availability and absence of a STROBE flow diagram or protocol pre-specification
Short-term composite endpoint only; no oncological or long-term outcomes to substantiate claims about expert-hand superiority
chief_reviewer.rationale: A competently reported but methodologically modest single-center retrospective PSM analysis whose central comparison is confounded by surgeon experience and era; it fits a tier-3 oncology/surgical journal after substantive revisions that address trainee imbalance and temporal bias with sensitivity analyses.
